source("../../_shared/template/polaris_rmd_helpers.R")
Sys.setenv(VELKSCALA_ROOT = "E:/Active Projects/Project 1746 - Intellte/papers/velkscala")
source("E:/Active Projects/Project 1746 - Intellte/core/framework/R/framework_init.R")

orig_render_figure_template <- render_figure_template
render_figure_template <- function (arg0_file_path, arg1_options = NULL) {
  options <- if (!is.null(arg1_options)) arg1_options else list()
  options$placement <- "!htbp"
  if (is.null(options$max_height) || identical(options$max_height, "none")) {
    options$max_height <- "0.42\\textheight"
  }
  return(orig_render_figure_template(arg0_file_path, options))
}
```

"russia_southern_far_east_pacific_primorye_khabarovsk_amur_sakhalin",   "Nakhodka-Russia": "russia_southern_far_east_pacific_primorye_khabarovsk_amur_sakhalin",   "Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk-Russia": "russia_southern_far_east_pacific_primorye_khabarovsk_amur_sakhalin",   "Ussuriysk-Russia": "russia_southern_far_east_pacific_primorye_khabarovsk_amur_sakhalin",   "Birobidzhan-Russia": "russia_southern_far_east_pacific_primorye_khabarovsk_amur_sakhalin" }', simplifyVector = FALSE)
sum_p <- if (file.exists((if (file.exists("post_soviet_space_summary.json")) "post_soviet_space_summary.json" else "../../_shared/_gis_cache/post_soviet_space_summary.json"))) (if (file.exists("post_soviet_space_summary.json")) "post_soviet_space_summary.json" else "../../_shared/_gis_cache/post_soviet_space_summary.json") else (if (file.exists("post_soviet_space_summary.json")) "post_soviet_space_summary.json" else "../../_shared/_gis_cache/post_soviet_space_summary.json")

strip_trailing_zeroes <- function(s) {
  s <- sub(",([1-9]+)0+$", ",\\1", s)
  s <- sub(",0+$", "", s)
  s
}

fmt_eu_pop <- function(val) {
  if (is.null(val) || is.na(val)) return("-")
  v <- as.numeric(val)
  if (v <= 0) return("-")
  if (v >= 1000000) {
    m <- round(v / 1000000, 2)
    s <- strip_trailing_zeroes(gsub("\\.", ",", format(m, nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE)))
    return(paste0(s, "M"))
  }
  if (v >= 1000) {
    k <- round(v / 1000, 1)
    s <- strip_trailing_zeroes(gsub("\\.", ",", format(k, nsmall = 1, trim = TRUE)))
    return(paste0(s, "k"))
  }
  return(as.character(as.integer(round(v))))
}

fmt_eu_coord <- function(x) {
  s <- gsub("\\.", ",", format(round(as.numeric(x), 2), nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE))
  strip_trailing_zeroes(s)
}

get_entry_pop <- function(entry, yr_str) {
  p <- entry$population[[yr_str]]
  if (is.null(p)) return(NA_real_)
  as.numeric(p)
}

fmt_pct_change <- function(entry) {
  p1 <- get_entry_pop(entry, "1991")
  p2 <- get_entry_pop(entry, "2021")
  if (is.na(p1) || is.na(p2) || p1 <= 0) return("Abandoned")
  pct <- round((p2 - p1) / p1 * 100, 1)
  sign_s <- if (pct > 0) "+" else ""
  if (abs(pct) >= 1000) {
    k <- round(pct / 1000, 2)
    s <- strip_trailing_zeroes(gsub("\\.", ",", format(k, nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE)))
    return(paste0(sign_s, s, "k%"))
  }
  s <- strip_trailing_zeroes(gsub("\\.", ",", format(pct, nsmall = 1, trim = TRUE)))
  paste0(sign_s, s, "%")
}

hyphenate_long_name <- function(nm) {
  s <- as.character(nm)
  s <- gsub("Sievierodonetsk", "Sievierodo-netsk", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("Kostiantynivka", "Kostianty-nivka", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("Nizhnevartovsk", "Nizhnevar-tovsk", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("Severobaykalsk", "Severobay-kalsk", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("Blagoveshchensk", "Blagovesh-chensk", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("Dnipropetrovsk", "Dnipropet-rovsk", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("Novocherkassk", "Novocher-kassk", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("Verkhneudinsk", "Verkhne-udinsk", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky", "Petropav-lovsk-Kamchatsky", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("\u041a\u0440\u0430\u0441\u043d\u043e\u043a\u0430\u043c\u0435\u043d\u0441\u043a", "\u041a\u0440\u0430\u0441\u043d\u043e-\u043a\u0430\u043c\u0435\u043d\u0441\u043a", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("\u0421\u0435\u0432\u0435\u0440\u043e\u0431\u0430\u0439\u043a\u0430\u043b\u044c\u0441\u043a", "\u0421\u0435\u0432\u0435\u0440\u043e-\u0431\u0430\u0439\u043a\u0430\u043b\u044c\u0441\u043a", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("([[:alpha:]]{8})([[:alpha:]]{6,})", "\\1-\\2", s, perl = TRUE)
  s
}

build_region_df <- function(reg_slug) {
  sub_list <- Filter(function(e) identical(as.character(reg35_map[[e$key]]), as.character(reg_slug)), all_entries)
  rows <- lapply(sub_list, function(e) {
    raw_oth <- if (length(e$other_names) > 0) unlist(e$other_names) else character(0)
    if (length(raw_oth) > 1) {
      oth <- paste(head(raw_oth, 2L), collapse = "; ")
    } else if (length(raw_oth) == 1) {
      oth <- raw_oth[1]
    } else {
      oth <- "-"
    }
    coords_span <- paste0(
      fmt_eu_coord(e$coords[[1]]), ", ", fmt_eu_coord(e$coords[[2]]),
      " (", e$country, ")"
    )
    data.frame(
      `Settlement` = hyphenate_long_name(e$name),
      `Other Names` = hyphenate_long_name(oth),
      `Coords` = coords_span,
      `1991` = fmt_eu_pop(get_entry_pop(e, "1991")),
      `2002` = fmt_eu_pop(get_entry_pop(e, "2002")),
      `2010` = fmt_eu_pop(get_entry_pop(e, "2010")),
      `2014` = fmt_eu_pop(get_entry_pop(e, "2014")),
      `2021` = fmt_eu_pop(get_entry_pop(e, "2021")),
      `Change` = fmt_pct_change(e),
      check.names = FALSE,
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  })
  do.call(rbind, rows)
}
```

```{=latex}
\emergencystretch=1.5em
```

# Abstract

Between the dissolution of the Soviet Union in December 1991 and the eve of the full-scale Russo-Ukrainian war in late 2021, the total population across Belarus, Ukraine and the Russian Federation declined by 14,18M (-6,7%), falling from 212,26M to 198,08M. Beneath this overall contraction, however, the urban hierarchy of the post-Soviet space underwent a marked spatial polarisation. Across the 234 major towns and cities catalogued in this gazetteer, the combined urban population rose by 6% from 91,07M in 1991 to 96,49M in 2021 as migrants moved from shrinking rural districts, mono-industrial towns and high-latitude settlements toward metropolitan, sunbelt and hydrocarbon growth poles.

This gazetteer traces the population histories of those 234 settlements across the 35 demographic regions of Belarus (Regions 1-3), Ukraine (Regions 4-11) and the Russian Federation (Regions 12-35) at five benchmark dates: 1991, 2002, 2010, 2014 and 2021. The regional tables contrast the rapid expansion of Moscow, Saint Petersburg, Krasnodar, Makhachkala, Surgut, Tyumen, Kyiv and Minsk against the contraction of Arctic mining towns in Chukotka, Magadan, Norilsk and Vorkuta, coal-basin centres in the Kuzbass and the war-torn cities of Chechnya and the Donbas.

# Methodology

This gazetteer covers 234 urban settlements across the 35 regions of Belarus (Regions 1-3), Ukraine within its 1991 borders (Regions 4-11, separating Government-Controlled Donbas in Region 9, Pre-2022 Occupied Donbas in Region 10 and Crimea and Sevastopol in Region 11) and the Russian Federation (Regions 12-35, including the North Caucasus in Regions 22-24 and Siberia and the Far East in Regions 26-35). Each regional table gives the settlement name, historical or alternative toponyms, coordinates and population estimates for 1991, 2002, 2010, 2014 and 2021.

Population figures draw on the 1999, 2009 and 2019 censuses of Belarus [@belstat2000perepis1999; @belstat2010perepis2009; @belstat2020perepis2019], the 2001 Ukrainian census, annual Ukrstat municipal series and the 2019 Electronic Population Assessment [@ukrstat2003perepis2001; @ukrstat2021naselennia; @dubilet2020assessment2019], and the 2002, 2010 and 2021 Russian censuses [@rosstat2004perepis2002; @rosstat2012perepis2010; @rosstat2022perepis2021]. For northern settlements abandoned during the post-Soviet exodus, such as the Kolyma coal-mining town of Kadykchan in Region 34 (10,3k in 1991 and 875 in 2002), figures are given up to the last inhabited benchmark before closure.

```{r fig1-md-only, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
if (!knitr::is_latex_output()) {
  render_figure_template(
    "figures/post_soviet_space_regional_map.png",
    list(
      caption = "Distribution of the 234 catalogued urban settlements across the 35 demographic regions of Belarus, Ukraine and the Russian Federation, showing metropolitan growth poles and northern contraction zones between 1991 and 2021.",
      label = "fig:hero-map",
      span_columns = TRUE
    )
  )
}
```

# Results

## Minsk Metropolitan Region

Sustained migration into the Belarusian capital lifted the population of Minsk City and Minsk Oblast (Region 1) from 3,4M in 1991 to 3,48M in 2021 (+2,4%), with Minsk itself passing the two-million mark while surrounding industrial towns held steady (Table \ref{tab:reg1-sites}) [@belstat2020perepis2019].

```{r table-reg1, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
df_reg1 <- build_region_df("belarus_minsk_city_and_oblast_magnet")
render_table_template(
  df_reg1,
  list(
    caption = "Population of Minsk and principal towns in Minsk Oblast (Region 1), 1991-2021.",
    label = "tab:reg1-sites"
  )
)
```

## Western Belarus

Across Brest and Grodno oblasts (Region 2), overall population declined by -11,9% from 2,68M in 1991 to 2,36M in 2021, although the regional capitals of Grodno and Brest continued to grow through rural-to-urban migration (Table \ref{tab:reg2-sites}) [@belstat2020perepis2019].

```{r table-reg2, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
df_reg2 <- build_region_df("belarus_western_brest_and_grodno")
render_table_template(
  df_reg2,
  list(
    caption = "Urban populations in Brest and Grodno oblasts (Region 2), 1991-2021.",
    label = "tab:reg2-sites"
  )
)
```

## Eastern and Southeastern Belarus

Post-Chernobyl resettlement in Gomel and Mogilev and severe rural ageing in Vitebsk reduced the population of Eastern and Southeastern Belarus (Region 3) by -20,6%, from 4,17M in 1991 to 3,31M in 2021 (Table \ref{tab:reg3-sites}) [@belstat2020perepis2019].

```{r table-reg3, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
df_reg3 <- build_region_df("belarus_eastern_vitebsk_mogilev_gomel")
render_table_template(
  df_reg3,
  list(
    caption = "Urban populations across Vitebsk, Mogilev and Gomel oblasts (Region 3), 1991-2021.",
    label = "tab:reg3-sites"
  )
)
```

## Western Ukraine and Transcarpathia

Higher rural fertility across Galicia, Volhynia, Bukovina and Zakarpattia (Region 4) cushioned labour emigration to the European Union, limiting regional contraction to -9,1% (from 10,25M in 1991 to 9,32M in 2021; Table \ref{tab:reg4-sites}) [@ukrstat2021naselennia].

```{r table-reg4, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
df_reg4 <- build_region_df("ukraine_western_galicia_volhynia_carpathians")
render_table_template(
  df_reg4,
  list(
    caption = "Population of Lviv and regional centres in Galicia, Volhynia, Bukovina and Zakarpattia (Region 4), 1991-2021.",
    label = "tab:reg4-sites"
  )
)
```

## Kyiv and the Metropolitan Ring

Kyiv City and Kyiv Oblast (Region 5) formed the sole demographic growth pole in post-Soviet Ukraine, expanding by +4,6% from 4,58M in 1991 to 4,79M in 2021 as Kyiv and its suburban ring (Brovary, Irpin and Bucha) absorbed internal migrants and displaced residents from the east (Table \ref{tab:reg5-sites}) [@ukrstat2021naselennia; @dubilet2020assessment2019].

```{r table-reg5, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
df_reg5 <- build_region_df("ukraine_kyiv_city_and_metropolitan_oblast")
render_table_template(
  df_reg5,
  list(
    caption = "Population of Kyiv and its suburban commuter towns in Kyiv Oblast (Region 5), 1991-2021.",
    label = "tab:reg5-sites"
  )
)
```

## Central and Northern Ukraine

Pronounced rural ageing and out-migration across the eight oblasts of Central and Northern Ukraine (Region 6) drove regional population down by -25,5%, from 12,12M in 1991 to 9,03M in 2021 (Table \ref{tab:reg6-sites}) [@ukrstat2021naselennia].

```{r table-reg6, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}

render_table_template(
  df_reg6,
  list(
    caption = "Population of oblast capitals and secondary towns across Central and Northern Ukraine (Region 6), 1991-2021.",
    label = "tab:reg6-sites"
  )
)
```

## Kharkiv, Dnipro and Zaporizhzhia

Across Ukraine's Dnieper-Slobozhanshchyna industrial belt (Region 7), heavy-industrial restructuring and natural decrease reduced the regional population by -20,3% from 9,1M in 1991 to 7,25M in 2021 (Table \ref{tab:reg7-sites}) [@ukrstat2021naselennia].

```{r table-reg7, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}

    label = "tab:reg7-sites"
  )
)
```

## Ukrainian Black Sea Littoral

The maritime oblasts of Odesa, Mykolaiv and Kherson (Region 8) contracted by -13,8% from 4,7M in 1991 to 4,05M in 2021, with Odesa holding near one million inhabitants while shipbuilding and port towns on the Southern Bug and lower Dnieper shrank (Table \ref{tab:reg8-sites}) [@ukrstat2021naselennia].

```{r table-reg8, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}

    label = "tab:reg8-sites"
  )
)
```

## Government-Controlled Donbas

In the Ukrainian-held districts of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts west and north of the 2014-2021 Line of Contact (Region 9), post-Soviet coal-basin shrinkage and wartime displacement reduced the population by -39%, from 3,62M in 1991 to 2,21M in 2021 (Table \ref{tab:reg9-sites}) [@ukrstat2021naselennia].

```{r table-reg9, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}

render_table_template(

  list(
    caption = "Population of Mariupol, Kramatorsk, Sievierodonetsk and frontline towns in Government-Controlled Donbas (Region 9), 1991-2021.",
    label = "tab:reg9-sites"
  )
)
```

## Occupied Donbas

Across the occupied Donetsk-Makiivka-Horlivka and Luhansk-Alchevsk conurbations (Region 10), wartime flight after April 2014 and acute natural decrease reduced the regional total by -46,3%, from 4,6M in 1991 to 2,47M in 2021 (Table \ref{tab:reg10-sites}) [@ukrstat2021naselennia; @gladun2020ukraine].

```{r table-reg10, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}

render_table_template(

    label = "tab:reg10-sites"
  )
)
```

## Crimea and Sevastopol

In Crimea and Sevastopol (Region 11), the population stood at 2,44M in 2021 (-3,6% relative to 2,53M in 1991), as post-2014 military and civilian inflows from the Russian Federation lifted Sevastopol from 344k in 2014 to 548k in 2021 (Table \ref{tab:reg11-sites}) [@ukrstat2021naselennia; @rosstat2022perepis2021].

```{r table-reg11, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}

    label = "tab:reg11-sites"
  )
)
```

## Moscow City and Oblast

As the primary destination of internal and international migration in the Russian Federation, Moscow City and Moscow Oblast (Region 12) expanded by +33,9% from 15,8M in 1991 to 21,15M in 2021, with rapid growth across the outer commuter ring led by Balashikha, Podolsk, Khimki and Mytishchi (Table \ref{tab:reg12-sites}) [@rosstat2022perepis2021].

```{r table-reg12, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}

render_table_template(
  df_reg12,
  list(
    caption = "Population of Moscow and its principal satellite cities in Moscow Oblast (Region 12), 1991-2021.",
    label = "tab:reg12-sites"
  )
)
```

## Saint Petersburg, Leningrad and Kaliningrad

Sustained in-migration lifted Saint Petersburg, Leningrad Oblast and the Kaliningrad exclave (Region 13) by +10,5% from 7,62M in 1991 to 8,42M in 2021, including the rapid growth of suburban Murino on the northern edge of Saint Petersburg (Table \ref{tab:reg13-sites}) [@rosstat2022perepis2021].

```{r table-reg13, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}

    label = "tab:reg13-sites"
  )
)
```

## Northwestern Russia and Karelia

Severe rural ageing and out-migration toward Saint Petersburg and Moscow reduced the population of Pskov, Novgorod, Vologda and Karelia (Region 14) by -24,7%, from 3,72M in 1991 to 2,8M in 2021 (Table \ref{tab:reg14-sites}) [@rosstat2022perepis2021].

## European Russian Arctic

Across Murmansk and Arkhangelsk oblasts, the Komi Republic and the Nenets Autonomous Okrug (Region 15), the post-Soviet northern outflow reduced regional population by -36,1% from 4,32M in 1991 to 2,76M in 2021, with coal-mining towns in the Pechora basin (Vorkuta and Inta) losing more than half their residents (Table \ref{tab:reg15-sites}) [@rosstat2022perepis2021].

    label = "tab:reg15-sites"
  )
)
```

## Central Non-Black-Earth Region

In the eleven oblasts surrounding the Moscow region (Region 16), high mortality and youth out-migration to the capital reduced the regional total by -21,1% from 12,35M in 1991 to 9,75M in 2021, accompanied by steady contraction in older textile and engineering centres such as Ivanovo, Tula and Rybinsk (Table \ref{tab:reg16-sites}) [@rosstat2022perepis2021].

  )

## Central Black-Earth Region

Across the fertile *Chernozemye* oblasts of Belgorod, Voronezh, Kursk, Lipetsk, Orel and Tambov (Region 17), repatriation inflows during the 1990s and the growth of Voronezh and Belgorod moderated overall regional decline to -9,4%, from 7,75M in 1991 to 7,02M in 2021 (Table \ref{tab:reg17-sites}) [@rosstat2022perepis2021].

## Tatarstan and Bashkortostan

Supported by oil-refining, petrochemical industry and balanced natural and migratory trends, the republics of Tatarstan and Bashkortostan (Region 18) grew by +4,9% from 7,58M in 1991 to 7,95M in 2021, led by Kazan and Ufa (Table \ref{tab:reg18-sites}) [@rosstat2022perepis2021].

## Middle Volga and the Finno-Ugric Republics

Across Samara, Nizhny Novgorod, Kirov, Ulyanovsk and Penza oblasts alongside Chuvashia, Mari El, Mordovia and Udmurtia (Region 19), industrial restructuring and natural decrease reduced the regional population by -13,5%, from 15,4M in 1991 to 13,31M in 2021 (Table \ref{tab:reg19-sites}) [@rosstat2022perepis2021].

)

## Lower Volga and Kalmykia

Along the lower Volga valley in Saratov, Volgograd and Astrakhan oblasts and the Republic of Kalmykia (Region 20), early repatriation gains were followed by post-2000 natural decline, reducing the regional total by -9,6% from 7,12M in 1991 to 6,44M in 2021 (Table \ref{tab:reg20-sites}) [@rosstat2022perepis2021].

## Kuban, Don and Stavropol

Attracting both post-Soviet repatriates and retirees from northern Russia, the Southern Russian Sunbelt of Krasnodar and Stavropol krais, Rostov Oblast and Adygea (Region 21) expanded by +11,9% from 13,15M in 1991 to 14,71M in 2021, with Krasnodar crossing the one-million threshold alongside booming Sochi and Stavropol (Table \ref{tab:reg21-sites}) [@rosstat2022perepis2021].

```

## Chechnya and Ingushetia

Despite wartime devastation in Grozny during the Chechen Wars of 1994-2009 and the permanent departure of most ethnic Russian residents, high Vainakh natural increase and post-war reconstruction lifted Chechnya and Ingushetia (Region 22) by +54,5% from 1,32M in 1991 to 2,04M in 2021, while displaced arrivals swelled Nazran nearly sevenfold (Table \ref{tab:reg22-sites}) [@rosstat2022perepis2021].

```{r table-reg22, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
df_reg22 <- build_region_df("russia_chechnya_and_ingushetia_wars_and_rebound")
render_table_template(
  df_reg22,
  list(
    caption = "Population of Grozny, Nazran and urban centres in Chechnya and Ingushetia (Region 22), 1991-2021.",
    label = "tab:reg22-sites"
  )
)
```

## North Ossetia, Kabardino-Balkaria and Karachay-Cherkessia

Across the central North Caucasus republics of North Ossetia-Alania, Kabardino-Balkaria and Karachay-Cherkessia (Region 23), indigenous natural increase and refugee inflows from South Ossetia outweighed ethnic Russian out-migration, lifting the regional total by +9,9% from 1,92M in 1991 to 2,11M in 2021 (Table \ref{tab:reg23-sites}) [@rosstat2022perepis2021].

```{r table-reg23, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
df_reg23 <- build_region_df("russia_central_caucasus_ossetia_kabardino_karachay")
render_table_template(
  df_reg23,
  list(
    caption = "Population of Vladikavkaz, Nalchik, Cherkessk and Beslan in the central North Caucasus (Region 23), 1991-2021.",
    label = "tab:reg23-sites"
  )
)
```

## Republic of Dagestan

Sustained natural increase and mountain-to-piedmont migration made Dagestan (Region 24) the fastest-growing region in the post-Soviet space, expanding by +77,1% from 1,88M in 1991 to 3,33M in 2021 and nearly doubling the population of Makhachkala, Kaspiysk and Khasavyurt (Table \ref{tab:reg24-sites}) [@rosstat2022perepis2021].

```{r table-reg24, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
df_reg24 <- build_region_df("russia_dagestan_high_fertility_boom")
render_table_template(
  df_reg24,
  list(
    caption = "Population of Makhachkala, Khasavyurt, Derbent and Kaspiysk in Dagestan (Region 24), 1991-2021.",
    label = "tab:reg24-sites"
  )
)
```

## Ural Industrial Belt

Across Sverdlovsk, Chelyabinsk, Perm, Orenburg and Kurgan oblasts (Region 25), the growth of Yekaterinburg and Chelyabinsk nearly offset steep contraction in single-industry metallurgical and mining towns such as Nizhny Tagil, Zlatoust and Berezniki, limiting overall regional decline to -3,8% (from 16,32M in 1991 to 15,7M in 2021; Table \ref{tab:reg25-sites}) [@rosstat2022perepis2021].

```{r table-reg25, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
df_reg25 <- build_region_df("russia_ural_industrial_sverdlovsk_chelyabinsk_perm_orenburg_kurgan")
render_table_template(
  df_reg25,
  list(
    caption = "Population of Yekaterinburg, Chelyabinsk, Perm and industrial centres in the Urals (Region 25), 1991-2021.",
    label = "tab:reg25-sites"
  )
)
```

## Yugra and Yamal

Unlike the depopulating coal and metal-mining zones of the Russian North, the oil and gas autonomous okrugs of Khanty-Mansi (Yugra) and Yamalo-Nenets (Region 26) expanded by +23,9% from 1,82M in 1991 to 2,25M in 2021, led by Surgut, Nizhnevartovsk, Novy Urengoy and Khanty-Mansiysk (Table \ref{tab:reg26-sites}) [@rosstat2022perepis2021].

```{r table-reg26, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
df_reg26 <- build_region_df("russia_yugra_and_yamal_hydrocarbon_arctic")
render_table_template(
  df_reg26,
  list(
    caption = "Population of Surgut, Nizhnevartovsk, Novy Urengoy and administrative centres in Yugra and Yamal (Region 26), 1991-2021.",
    label = "tab:reg26-sites"
  )
)
```

## West Siberian Corridor

Along the West Siberian section of the Trans-Siberian Railway across Tyumen, Omsk, Novosibirsk and Tomsk oblasts and Altai Krai (Region 27), rapid growth in Tyumen, Novosibirsk and Tomsk cushioned rural and industrial losses elsewhere, holding overall contraction to -5,9% (from 11,15M in 1991 to 10,49M in 2021; Table \ref{tab:reg27-sites}) [@rosstat2022perepis2021].

```{r table-reg27, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
df_reg27 <- build_region_df("russia_west_siberia_transsiberian_tyumen_omsk_novosibirsk_tomsk_altai")
render_table_template(
  df_reg27,
  list(
    caption = "Population of Novosibirsk, Omsk, Tyumen, Barnaul and Tomsk in the West Siberian Corridor (Region 27), 1991-2021.",
    label = "tab:reg27-sites"
  )
)
```

## Kuzbass Coal Basin

Post-Soviet coal-mine closures and metallurgical restructuring across Kemerovo Oblast (Region 28) reduced the population of the Kuzbass by -18,2% from 3,18M in 1991 to 2,6M in 2021, with steep losses in Prokopyevsk and Kiselevsk alongside moderate contraction in Novokuznetsk and Kemerovo (Table \ref{tab:reg28-sites}) [@rosstat2022perepis2021].

```{r table-reg28, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
df_reg28 <- build_region_df("russia_kuzbass_kemerovo_coal_restructuring")
render_table_template(
  df_reg28,
  list(
    caption = "Population of Novokuznetsk, Kemerovo, Prokopyevsk and Kiselevsk in the Kuzbass coal basin (Region 28), 1991-2021.",
    label = "tab:reg28-sites"
  )
)
```

## Altai, Khakassia and Tuva

In the southern Siberian republics of Altai, Khakassia and Tuva (Region 29), above-replacement Tuvan and Altai fertility offset ethnic Russian out-migration, keeping the regional population nearly unchanged at 1,08M in 2021 (-0,5% from 1,09M in 1991) while lifting Kyzyl, Abakan and Gorno-Altaysk (Table \ref{tab:reg29-sites}) [@rosstat2022perepis2021].

```{r table-reg29, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
df_reg29 <- build_region_df("russia_altai_khakassia_and_tuva_republics")
render_table_template(
  df_reg29,
  list(
    caption = "Population of Abakan, Kyzyl, Chernogorsk and Gorno-Altaysk in southern Siberia (Region 29), 1991-2021.",
    label = "tab:reg29-sites"
  )
)
```

## East Siberian Corridor

Along the Angara-Yenisei industrial corridor in Krasnoyarsk Krai and Irkutsk Oblast (Region 30), the growth of Krasnoyarsk past one million inhabitants contrasted with contraction in timber and aluminium towns such as Bratsk and Angarsk, reducing the regional total by -14,3% from 6,03M in 1991 to 5,17M in 2021 (Table \ref{tab:reg30-sites}) [@rosstat2022perepis2021].

```{r table-reg30, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}

render_table_template(

  list(
    caption = "Population of Krasnoyarsk, Irkutsk, Angarsk and Bratsk in the East Siberian Corridor (Region 30), 1991-2021.",
    label = "tab:reg30-sites"
  )
)
```

## Norilsk, Taymyr and Evenkia

In the polar mining and timber district of Norilsk, Taymyr and Evenkia in northern Krasnoyarsk Krai (Region 31), the curtailment of northern labour subsidies reduced the regional population by -42,1%, from 380k in 1991 to 220k in 2021 (Table \ref{tab:reg31-sites}) [@rosstat2022perepis2021].

```{r table-reg31, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}

    label = "tab:reg31-sites"
  )
)
```

## Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai

Across Transbaikalia in the Republic of Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai (Region 32), rural-to-urban migration lifted Ulan-Ude by nearly a quarter even as westward out-migration reduced the overall regional population by -17,2%, from 2,41M in 1991 to 2M in 2021 (Table \ref{tab:reg32-sites}) [@rosstat2022perepis2021].

```{r table-reg32, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}

render_table_template(

    label = "tab:reg32-sites"
  )
)
```

## Sakha Republic (Yakutia)

In the Sakha Republic (Region 33), the exodus of ethnic Russian workers from northern mining and Arctic port settlements such as Neryungri and Tiksi was largely counterbalanced by high rural Sakha fertility and migration into Yakutsk, which nearly doubled between 1991 and 2021 and held overall regional contraction to -11,3% (from 1,11M to 985k; Table \ref{tab:reg33-sites}) [@rosstat2022perepis2021].

```{r table-reg33, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}

render_table_template(

  list(
    caption = "Population of Yakutsk, Neryungri, Mirny and Tiksi in the Sakha Republic (Region 33), 1991-2021.",
    label = "tab:reg33-sites"
  )
)
```

## Magadan, Chukotka and Kamchatka

Across the northeast Arctic and sub-Arctic belt of Magadan Oblast, Chukotka Autonomous Okrug and Kamchatka Krai (Region 34), the post-Soviet northern exodus reduced the regional population by more than half (-52,9%, from 1,03M in 1991 to 485k in 2021) and left Kolyma mining settlements such as Kadykchan completely abandoned (Table \ref{tab:reg34-sites}) [@rosstat2022perepis2021].

```{r table-reg34, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}

render_table_template(

  list(
    caption = "Population of Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky, Magadan, Anadyr and Kolyma mining towns (Region 34), 1991-2021.",
    label = "tab:reg34-sites"
  )
)
```

## Southern Far East and the Pacific Littoral

Across Primorsky and Khabarovsk krais, Amur and Sakhalin oblasts and the Jewish Autonomous Oblast (Region 35), sustained westward out-migration reduced the regional population by -24,3% from 6,06M in 1991 to 4,58M in 2021, with Khabarovsk, Vladivostok, Blagoveshchensk and Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk holding steady while defence and port towns such as Komsomolsk-on-Amur and Nakhodka contracted (Table \ref{tab:reg35-sites}) [@rosstat2022perepis2021].

```{r table-reg35, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}

  list(
    caption = "Population of Vladivostok, Khabarovsk, Blagoveshchensk and Pacific littoral cities (Region 35), 1991-2021.",
    label = "tab:reg35-sites"
  )
)
```

# Appendix

## Regional Gazetteer Summary

Table \ref{tab:regional-summary} summarises the number of urban settlements covered in each of the 35 regions and their combined urban population from 1991 to 2021. Across all 234 cities and towns, total urban population rose from 91,07M in 1991 to 96,49M in 2021 (+6%), reflecting demographic concentration into metropolitan agglomerations (Regions 1, 5, 12, 13, 18, 21, 24 and 26) even as rural districts, conflict zones (Regions 9, 10 and 22) and northern or coal-mining *monogoroda* (Regions 15, 28, 31, 34 and 35) contracted.

```{r table-summary, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
bench_yrs <- c("1991", "2002", "2010", "2014", "2021")

sum_rows <- lapply(seq_along(summary_meta$regions), function(idx) {
  reg <- summary_meta$regions[[idx]]
  rslug <- as.character(reg$id)
  sub_e <- Filter(function(e) identical(as.character(reg35_map[[e$key]]), rslug), all_entries)
  raw_sums <- sapply(bench_yrs, function(y) {
    vals <- sapply(sub_e, function(e) {
      v <- get_entry_pop(e, y)
      if (is.na(v)) 0 else v
    })
    sum(vals)
  })
  sums <- sapply(raw_sums, fmt_eu_pop)
  pct <- round((raw_sums[["2021"]] - raw_sums[["1991"]]) / raw_sums[["1991"]] * 100, 1)
  pct_s <- paste0(if (pct > 0) "+" else "", strip_trailing_zeroes(gsub("\\.", ",", format(pct, nsmall = 1, trim = TRUE))), "%")
  clean_reg_nm <- sub("\\s*\\(.*", "", as.character(reg$name))
  clean_reg_nm <- gsub("([0-9])AD\\b", "\\1", clean_reg_nm)
  clean_reg_nm <- gsub("Dnipropetrovsk", "Dnipro-petrovsk", clean_reg_nm, fixed = TRUE)
  clean_reg_nm <- gsub("Arkhangelsk", "Arkhan-gelsk", clean_reg_nm, fixed = TRUE)
  data.frame(
    `Region (Cities)` = paste0(clean_reg_nm, " (", length(sub_e), ")"),
    `1991` = sums[["1991"]],
    `2002` = sums[["2002"]],
    `2010` = sums[["2010"]],
    `2014` = sums[["2014"]],
    `2021` = sums[["2021"]],
    `Change` = pct_s,
    check.names = FALSE,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_sum <- do.call(rbind, sum_rows)

tot_raw <- sapply(bench_yrs, function(y) {
  vals <- sapply(all_entries, function(e) {
    v <- get_entry_pop(e, y)
    if (is.na(v)) 0 else v
  })
  sum(vals)
})
tot_sums <- sapply(tot_raw, fmt_eu_pop)
tot_pct <- round((tot_raw[["2021"]] - tot_raw[["1991"]]) / tot_raw[["1991"]] * 100, 1)
tot_pct_s <- paste0(if (tot_pct > 0) "+" else "", strip_trailing_zeroes(gsub("\\.", ",", format(tot_pct, nsmall = 1, trim = TRUE))), "%")

tot_row <- data.frame(
  `Region (Cities)` = paste0("Total Gazetteer Sample (", length(all_entries), ")"),
  `1991` = tot_sums[["1991"]],
  `2002` = tot_sums[["2002"]],
  `2010` = tot_sums[["2010"]],
  `2014` = tot_sums[["2014"]],
  `2021` = tot_sums[["2021"]],
  `Change` = tot_pct_s,
  check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
df_sum <- rbind(df_sum, tot_row)

render_table_template(
  df_sum,
  list(
    caption = "Combined urban population across all 234 catalogued settlements by region from 1991 to 2021.",
    label = "tab:regional-summary"
  )
)
```
